newsitem.title: USA: Clinton predicts UPS strike will settle soon.
newsitem.headline: Clinton predicts UPS strike will settle soon.

text.p: President Bill Clinton expressed optimism on Sunday that the Teamsters union and United Parcel Service were very close to settling their two-week-old dispute, but Teamsters President Ron Carey was less certain.

"It's my gut feeling they'll settle," Clinton told reporters as he arrived at Martha's Vineyard in Massachusetts for a three-week vacation. "They're that close," he said, holding up two fingers not very far apart.
"It's a good deal," Clinton told reporters "It will set a precedent for unions."

Company and union negotiators continued marathon meetings which began Thursday -- with only brief breaks for sleep -- at a hotel across the street from the International Brotherhood of Teamsters headquarters.
During a short break, Carey urged his members to keep up the pressure. He spoke in a conference call to more than 200 locals, where rank-and-file members were listening with union officials.

"We still don't have agreements on any major issue," Carey said. He exhorted his members to prepare for everything from candlelight vigils to distributing leaflets at sports events this week to build support for the strike.
A White House official said if no agreement was reached overnight the talks would end for now.

Deputy White House counsel Bruce Lindsey told reporters traveling with Clinton if the parties could not reach agreement, then Labor Secretary Alexis Herman would call for a recess to allow negotiators to get some rest.
Herman, who was credited by both sides with helping to keep the talks moving, was scheduled to fly to Los Angeles on Monday for a speaking engagement.
The walkout by drivers, loaders and sorters on Aug. 4 has crippled the nation's largest package delivery firm, costing the company an estimated $600 million so far.
Clinton expressed concern earlier in the day about the wide-ranging impact of the strike, saying it was "beginning to hurt not only the company but its employees and the people who depend on it."
UPS competitors, including the U.S. Postal Service, have rushed to fill the void. But many small businesses are feeling the pinch of being unable to have their goods delivered.
UPS officials this week responded to a request by the Federal Reserve Board, sending officials a detailed analysis of the strike's impact on the company and the economy.

UPS Chairman James Kelly, appearing on NBC's "Meet the Press," sounded an optimistic, though cautious note, saying that negotiators were discussing "dozens and dozens of issues" but it was unclear when an agreement could be reached.
"The fact that we're continuing to talk is encouraging," Kelly said, repeating that the company would use replacement workers only as a last resort.
"We've been at make or break points a number of times before," Kelly told CNN later on Sunday. "Perhaps we're at another one right now."
Carey said on the NBC program that the talks had made progresss for the first time since they began.
"There has been some movement," he said.
Buoyed by opinion polls showing the strikers winning the public relations battle, Carey has stuck to his theme that UPS convert more part-time jobs into higher paying full-time jobs.

For its part, UPS has insisted on establishing a new pension fund -- which would cover only UPS workers -- to replace the existing fund covering Teamster workers at dozens of companies, mostly trucking lines.
The strikers were getting help from other unions, but were finding it tough to live on $55-a-week strike benefits.
The strike is the largest since a three-day 1976 strike by 400,000 Teamster truck drivers, according to Cornell University labor studies professor Richard Hurd.
